questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Greeting and the part of day it uses
questions.learningObjective: say which part of the day a greeting belongs to
questions.stem: A shop assistant greets a customer at nine in the morning with 'Buenos días, ¿qué tal?' and the customer answers 'Muy bien, gracias.' What is the assistant's greeting doing in that exchange?

options.text: It marks the part of the day before noon, since días is used from dawn until midday
It marks a friendliness that lasts all day, since días covers every hour until closing
options.misconception: reads the English sense of a whole day into the Spanish part of day

options.text: It marks a formal occasion, since días is kept for greetings on paper rather than speech
options.misconception: takes the choice of part of day as a marker of written formality

options.text: It marks the start of a friendship, since tal is only ever said at a first meeting
options.misconception: reads the reply qué tal as a phrase reserved for a first meeting

questions.explanation: Spanish divides the day into three named parts and the greeting has to match the hour at which it is spoken: días from dawn until about noon, tarde for the afternoon and the early evening, and noche for the rest. At nine in the morning días is the right word, and the reply qué tal may be used at any hour, so nothing in that phrase marks a first meeting. The trap is the English good day, which is a wish for the whole day; a speaker who transfers that meaning expects días to work in the evening as well, and sounds odd when they use it. The three words are not interchangeable, and the hour decides which one a native speaker reaches for.
questions.hint: Ask how many parts of the day Spanish names, and which of them contains nine in the morning.

questions.topic: Introducing yourself and the register that fits
questions.learningObjective: choose the introduction that matches the relationship being opened
questions.stem: Two candidates meet a panel for the first time. The first says 'Hola, me llamo Raúl, soy de Cáceres.' The second says 'Encantado de conocerle. Me llamo Raúl. Soy de Cáceres.' Which opening is the right one for that room?

options.text: The second one, because usted with a formal greeting is what an interview panel expects
The first one, because the tú form keeps the interview relaxed and puts the panel at ease
options.misconception: assumes that informality reassures a panel, when it reads as a mismatch of respect

options.text: The second one, because naming a place of origin is never suitable when meeting an employer
options.misconception: treats a place of origin as information no professional meeting should contain

options.text: The first one, because a first meeting should be opened by a question rather than a name
options.misconception: supposes a name cannot open an introduction and a question must come first

questions.explanation: The pronoun and the verb ending travel together, so the choice between the second person and the formal third person is a choice about distance, and distance is chosen by the setting rather than by the speaker's mood. A panel meeting sits at the formal end, where the third person and the greeting encantado de conocerle are unmarked and the tú form is read as a failure to read the room. The place of origin, by contrast, is ordinary in a Spanish introduction between strangers of any age, so it is not what makes an introduction unsuitable here. What separates the two openings is not warmth but respect, and a learner who assumes Spanish is uniformly informal mistakes a social signal for a stylistic choice.
questions.hint: Ask which pronoun a panel expects a candidate to be addressing, and which verb ending goes with it.

questions.topic: Ordering food and the phrases that do it
questions.learningObjective: recognise a complete order in a restaurant exchange
questions.stem: A waiter asks '¿Qué va a tomar?' and a diner answers 'Para mí, una fabada mallorquina y un vaso de agua, por favor.' What is the diner doing in that reply?

options.text: Ordering a dish and a drink, with a courtesy formula closing the request
Asking the waiter to recommend something, since va a tomar asks the diner a question
options.misconception: reads the waiter's what are you having as an invitation to ask advice

options.text: Checking that the waiter heard correctly, by giving the order back to him
options.misconception: treats a full order as a repetition rather than as the first statement

options.text: Declining to order, since naming dishes outright is heard as a refusal at table
options.misconception: assumes that stating what one wants counts as turning the order down

questions.explanation: The question va a tomar asks what the diner is having, so the answer has to name what the diner wants, and it does: a set dish named by its place of origin and a glass of water. The opening para mí assigns the order to one person at the table, which is what a group ordering needs, and the closing por favor supplies the courtesy that a request to a stranger requires. The order of the elements is also idiomatic, with the request formula last rather than first, and a learner who puts por favor at the front sounds as though apologising for ordering at all. A named dish and a named drink are the two halves of a complete order in Spanish.
questions.hint: Ask whether the waiter asked what the diner wanted, and whether the reply names it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Directions and the answer that gives them
questions.learningObjective: check a set of spoken directions against what was actually said
questions.stem: A visitor asks '¿Dónde está la plaza mayor?' and is answered 'Continúe derecho por dos calles, luego gire a la derecha y la verá a la izquierda.' Which restatement of those directions is accurate?

options.text: Go straight for two streets, then turn right and the square is on your left
Go straight for two streets, then turn left and the square is on your right
options.misconception: reverses the turn while keeping the word derecha, a common half-listened error

options.text: Walk two streets first, then double back and turn right at the square
options.misconception: turns a forward instruction into a return journey the speaker never mentioned

options.text: Go straight on until the square itself appears, and turn right only on arrival
options.misconception: puts the turn at the destination, where the instruction puts the landmark

questions.explanation: Spanish directions fix an order: the distance first, then the turn, then the landmark and the side it sits on. Here the order is two streets, a right turn, and the square on the left, and a listener who checks against that order can correct a mistake at once. The two mistakes that catch people are reversing the turn, which happens because derecha and izquierda are short and easy to swap when the speaker is already walking, and moving the turn to the end, which happens because a destination feels like the place where instructions belong. Both are habits of English directions rather than faults of Spanish, so the fix is to rehearse the sequence and the side.
questions.hint: Write down the three things the speaker said in the order the speaker said them.

questions.topic: Confirming that you have understood
questions.learningObjective: tell a confirmation back from a repetition
questions.stem: After a long explanation at a clinic reception, a patient says 'Entonces, si no entiendo mal, tengo que volver el jueves a las diez.' What is the patient doing with that sentence?

options.text: Checking the arrangement back in his own words, so that an error can be fixed now
Repeating the explanation exactly as heard, without adding a word of his own
options.misconception: reads a checking device as word-for-word recall of what was said

options.text: Asking a fresh question about what will happen later on that same Thursday
options.misconception: takes a restatement of an arrangement to be a new enquiry about the future

options.text: Expressing doubt about whether the clinic itself will still be open that day
options.misconception: moves a hedge attached to the patient's understanding onto the clinic's opening hours

A confirmation of that kind is worth a great deal in practical Spanish, because it costs the listener one sentence and can prevent a wrong day or a wrong hour, and the recipient is expected to answer the restatement rather than to repeat the original speech. The reason a learner misreads it is that a restatement looks like repetition, since the information is the same; what makes the difference is the hedge and the shift of the verb to the first person, which is a check and not a recall.

questions.topic: Asking someone to repeat
questions.learningObjective: choose the repeat request that keeps the exchange polite
questions.stem: A caller has not caught a telephone number and wants it again without sounding rude. Which sentence does that job?

options.text: ¿Me lo repite, por favor? Es que no he cogido el número.
¿Qué? Repita eso más alto, que aquí no se oye nada.
options.misconception: opens with a bare interrogative that reads as a reproach rather than a request

options.text: Repítamelo, pero hágalo con voz, porque así no entiendo nada.
options.misconception: makes the demand about the other person's voice, which is an insult in effect

options.text: Otra vez, porque no he entendido nada de lo que usted acaba de decir.
options.misconception: discards the request formula and puts the blame on the other's speech

The correct sentence has all three, and the reason no he cogido el número states plainly what went wrong without blame. Perdon and the formal imperative both appear in the distractors, which is what makes them sound severe: a bare imperativo with usted, with no softening, asks a stranger to do an extra piece of work for you and says nothing about why. questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Correcting yourself mid-sentence
questions.learningObjective: identify the device that withdraws a mistaken word in mid-sentence
questions.stem: A speaker begins 'Iba a decir que la reunión es el-' and then continues 'perdón, el jueves, no el martes.' Which device has the speaker used?

options.text: A self-correction marked by perdón, which withdraws the wrong day and substitutes the right one
A hesitation marked by a dash, which asks the listener to guess the missing word instead
options.misconception: reads the dash alone as a request for the listener to supply a word

options.text: A denial marked by no, which takes back the whole of what was said before the pause
options.misconception: treats a correction of one word as a retraction of the whole sentence

options.text: An apology for lateness, which explains why the first day named was mistaken
options.misconception: takes a correction of a noun as an apology for having arrived late

questions.explanation: A correction inside a sentence takes a small apology as a signal, and perdón is the one a speaker reaches for without interrupting the flow; the wrong item is then repeated with no, which cancels only that item. So el jueves, no el martes withdraws a single noun and the rest of the sentence stands. The dash alone is not a device for asking the listener to help, though it does mark that something was expected and has not arrived. A no that takes back everything would be a different act, since the speaker is not repudiating the sentence but correcting a word in it, and an apology for lateness would be an admission about the speaker's own conduct, which is a different fault altogether.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the sentence the speaker is withdrawing, and what word marks the switch.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Thanking and its two levels of formality
questions.learningObjective: tell a familiar thanksgiving from a deferential one
questions.stem: The same favour is thanked in two ways: 'Gracias por echarme una mano' to a friend, and 'Le agradezco mucho su ayuda' in a letter to an official. What separates the two expressions?

options.text: The register, since the first is familiar and warm and the second is deferential and formal
The size of the favour, since only a favour of some weight can be thanked for formally
options.misconception: supposes the choice of wording depends on how large the favour was

options.text: The tense, since thanking about the past requires a perfect tense in both expressions
options.misconception: believes the two differ in tense rather than in the level of formality

options.text: The word of thanks, since the second expression contains no word of gratitude at all
options.misconception: reads agradecer as a verb of thanks when it is a verb of acknowledging a debt

questions.explanation: Both expressions name the same act of receiving help, so what differs is the distance the speaker is willing to claim. The familiar one uses the second person, a prepositional phrase for the help, and a verb of liking, which is why it can end in a word of thanks as easily as not. The formal one uses the third person, the noun ayuda rather than a phrase, and a verb of gratitude, and it is the verb that carries the thanks in that sentence, so the absence of gracias is not a gap. The two are not graded by the size of the favour but by the relationship, which is why the same official gets the second in writing and might well receive the first in the corridor.
questions.hint: Ask which pronoun each expression uses, and what the relationship to the recipient requires.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Sorry and the apology it is not the same as
questions.learningObjective: separate an apology for a fault from a request to be allowed to pass
questions.stem: In 'Perdón, ¿puedo pasar?' said at a crowded bus door, and in 'Lo siento mucho, no quería hacerlo' said after spilling a drink, what does each word do?

options.text: Perdón asks to be let through, and lo siento admits a fault with real consequences
The two are interchangeable, and either will do in both of the situations described
options.misconception: assumes one word of apology covers an intrusion and an accident equally well

options.text: Lo siento excuses the speaker, and perdón admits the fault, which reverses the two
options.misconception: swaps which of the two words asks passage and which admits a fault

options.text: Perdón belongs to written messages, and lo siento is spoken in the street only
options.misconception: divides the two words by medium of communication rather than by meaning

questions.explanation: Spanish keeps two separate acts in two separate words, and the test is what the speaker is admitting. Perdón is used to interrupt, to get past someone, to begin an approach to a stranger, and to excuse a slip of the tongue; it concedes an imposition, not a fault, so the speaker at the bus door has not damaged anything and is not apologising for that. Lo siento is used when something has been done that the speaker regrets, and the addition of mucho marks how seriously the speaker takes the consequences. A learner who reaches for lo siento at a bus door is apologising for a crime that has not happened, and one who says perdón to a person whose drink is on the floor has failed to admit the fault at all.
questions.hint: Ask in each case what the speaker has done, and whether anything has been damaged.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A complaint and how it is escalated politely
questions.learningObjective: identify the move that raises the force of a complaint without being rude
questions.stem: A customer whose order arrived cold writes: 'He visto que mi pedido llegó frío. ¿Podrían enviarme otro? Quedo atenta.' Which move in that message does the escalating work?

options.text: The conditional request, which makes the demand a favour rather than an order
The opening observation, which states the fault before any politeness can soften it
options.misconception: believes the factual statement of the fault is the aggressive part of the letter

options.text: The closing formula, which thanks the firm and so withdraws the force of the request
options.misconception: takes a conventional letter closing to be a withdrawal of the complaint

options.text: The verb enviarme, which stays neutral and so leaves the severity to the reader
options.misconception: believes the choice of verb alone determines how strong the demand sounds

questions.explanation: The grammar of the request does the escalating. Podrían enviarme otro is built on the conditional, which places the action in the firm's own hands and gives it the form of an option rather than an order, so a firm that declines has said no to a possibility rather than refused an instruction. The opening clause is factual and has to stay factual, since a complaint that will not name the fault gives the reader nothing to act on; the closing queda atenta is a conventional ending that does not soften the middle. The reason a learner misjudges this is that the complaint sounds blunt before the question mark arrives, and the escalation only becomes visible once the request itself is examined.
questions.hint: Ask which grammar builds the request: an order, or an option offered to the reader?

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Asking someone's origin politely
questions.learningObjective: choose the question that asks origin and not residence
questions.stem: A new neighbour asks you, in Spanish, where you come from. Which question does that job correctly?

options.text: ¿De dónde es usted?
¿De dónde son sus padres?
options.misconception: asks about the parents' origin while sounding as though it asks about the listener's

options.text: ¿Dónde es usted de origen?
options.misconception: builds origin on dónde, which cannot take the preposition de with a question word

options.text: ¿De dónde está usted?
options.misconception: uses estar for origin, which asks where the person is rather than what they are

questions.explanation: Origin is a matter of what a person is, not of where a person happens to be, and the copula ser is the one that reports it: de dónde es usted. The two near-misses each break that rule in a different way. The question with dónde cannot carry the preposition de, because dónde and de dónde are separate interrogative words, so the second construction is not built. The question with estar asks about a position, which answers a different question entirely and is the reason a learner who has learned the verb for place reaches for it here. The first distractor shows the real trap: it asks a question the speaker did not intend, since origin is inherited and the parents' country may not be the listener's.
questions.hint: Ask whether the question reports what someone is or where someone happens to be.

questions.topic: Prices and number agreement
questions.learningObjective: make the verb agree with a plural noun in a price question
questions.stem: A shopper has picked up two shirts and wants the price of both. Which question is grammatically correct?

options.misconception: keeps the singular noun with a plural verb, a mismatch the ear rarely catches

options.text: ¿Cuánto cuesto estas camisas?

options.misconception: leaves a singular noun after a numeral, as though the number were decoration

questions.topic: Quantities in a request
questions.learningObjective: use a measure noun without an article when the quantity is already meant
questions.stem: At a shop the customer wants half a litre of milk. Which request gets the quantity right?

options.text: Quisiera medio litro de leche, por favor.
Quisiera la medio litro de leche, por favor.
options.misconception: gives medio a feminine article, as though the measure were a feminine noun

options.text: Quisiera medio litro de leches, por favor.
options.misconception: pluralises the measured substance, which turns one measure into several

options.text: Quisiera un medio litro de leche, por favor.
options.misconception: adds the indefinite article to a word that already measures the quantity

The conditional quisiera with a final por favor is the courteous frame for the whole request and adds nothing to the grammar of the quantity.

questions.learningObjective: make an adjective agree with a plural noun in a menu description

questions.topic: Gender of the minutes in a spoken time
questions.learningObjective: explain why the noun for minutes changes gender halfway through the hour

answer.exemplar: A time of day in Spanish is built from the hour, which is feminine, and the minutes, which change gender halfway through. Up to thirty the noun is masculine, so seven twenty is las siete y veinte minutos. From thirty-one onwards it is feminine, so seven forty is las siete y cuarenta minutos, and a quarter to eight is las ocho menos cuarto. A speaker who says siete y cuarenta minutos is applying the rule for the first half of the hour to the second half, and the sentence sounds like a translation of the English because English has no such split. The check to give a learner is one question: is the number of minutes above thirty? If it is, the noun is feminine; if it is not, it is masculine. The hour is feminine in every case, including la una, because the noun behind the number is a feminine one and uno only shows its masculine side when it stands alone as a number.

questions.explanation: Items like this are hard for learners because the rule is invisible in English, and the first job in explaining one is to show that the split exists before showing where it falls. The second job is to give a decision procedure rather than a list, because a list of times has to be memorised and a question can be answered. The third is to explain the one case that looks irregular, since la una in a time of day is feminine and a learner who has been taught that uno is masculine will otherwise conclude that the rule is broken. A useful check for a teacher is to ask the learner to say any two times in the same hour, one under thirty and one over, which exposes the error faster than any explanation.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the noun for the minutes when the number passes thirty.

An explanation has to make the decision sound like a single choice made early, because that is what it is in practice, and it has to mention that the region can decide it, since a learner who has met the formal third person used with a parent abroad will otherwise conclude the practice is an error. A useful test to give a learner is to count the sentences and to check who the reason is about: one sentence, and the reason is about the speaker, and the sentence is an excuse. Two sentences with a contrast, and the reason is about a cause outside the speaker's control, and the sentence is a justification.

answer.exemplar: The frame carries the offer and the content carries the demand, and the two do different work. ¿Le viene bien el jueves a las diez y media? proposes an hour and gives the other party a question they can answer no to. Por la mañana, en cambio, does not propose anything: it describes a period, and the other party now has to find a slot in it, which is work the speaker should have done. The two that are often confused are the bare hour and the hedged hour, because a learner hears más o menos as vagueness. It is not: a las diez y media más o menos keeps the proposal and adds tolerance, so it is warmer than the bare hour rather than less precise, and it tells the other party they need not arrive to the minute. The final point to make is intonation, since ¿le viene bien...? with a rising voice is a genuine question and the same words read flat can be heard as a statement of what has already been arranged.

questions.explanation: A learner who is offered por la mañana in exchange for a specific hour has been handed the work, and the explanation has to make that asymmetry visible rather than simply calling one phrase polite and the other not. The confusion about a hedge is the part worth labouring, because learners have been trained to treat a qualifier as a loss of precision, and in this frame it is the opposite: it keeps the proposal and lowers the cost of accepting it. The intonation point belongs in the explanation because it is the one part of the choice the writer cannot see, and a learner reading a transcript will otherwise assume the punctuation carries the whole meaning.
questions.hint: Ask who has to do the work of finding a time in each of the two sentences.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Writing a request and defending it
questions.learningObjective: write a request that works, and say which of its parts carries the work
questions.stem: Stage one: write a short email asking a housing office to confirm a repair date for a flat whose heating has failed. Stage two: say which part of your email does the work of getting an answer.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: Estimado señor Ruiz: Le escribo por la calefacción de mi vivienda, en la calle Mayor: lleva dos semanas sin funcionar. ¿Podrían confirmarme la fecha prevista de la reparación? La última visita del técnico fue el día 4 y desde entonces no he recibido ninguna noticia. Quedo a la espera de su respuesta. Un saludo, Ana Prat. Stage two: the part that does the work is the question built on a conditional, ¿podrían confirmarme la fecha prevista?, because it is the only sentence that can be answered yes or no and it names the one thing the office has to supply. The details around it are there to make the request reasonable, not to make it effective: a reader who can tell which flat, which fault and since when will answer, and a reader who cannot will not. What the email should not do is describe the inconvenience at length or hint at a complaint, because an office that thinks it is being complained at starts by looking for who is to blame, and the repair date is what the writer needs.

questions.explanation: The two stages fail in different ways, and asking only for the first produces a fluent email with no answer in it. A request that fails is usually one where the reader is not told what would count as a success, so the reply is a forwarding address or a form. A request that fails in the other direction is one where the frustration has taken up the space the request needed, and the office now has a problem to manage rather than a question to answer. Setting the two stages together is what forces a learner to notice the difference between politeness and effectiveness, since the most courteous version is not always the version that gets a date, and the most direct version is not always the one that gets read.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence in your own email the office can answer with a single date.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Refusing an invitation in writing without damage
questions.learningObjective: write a refusal that keeps the relationship, and check it
questions.stem: Stage one: refuse a wedding invitation in Spanish in a short message. Stage two: check your own message and say which two words do the softening.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: Manyas gracias por la invitación. Me encantaría ir, pero ya tengo un compromiso de familia que no puedo mover en esas fechas. Les deseo lo mejor. Stage two: the two words that do the softening are me and the verb that follows it. Me encantaría praises the invitation before turning it down, so the refusal is aimed at the date and not at the occasion, and a verb of willingness rather than a verb of inability means the person is not rejecting the hosts. The second half of the work is done by pero, which introduces the obstacle as something separate from the yes, and by the noun compromiso, which names a reason of a kind nobody argues with. A check worth applying to any written refusal is whether the reader could repeat the yes afterwards; if the only thing they can repeat is the no, the message has failed, however politely it is phrased.

questions.explanation: A written refusal is harder than a spoken one because there is no tone to soften the grammar, and the whole burden falls on the words. Learners who are told to be polite often produce a message with nothing but hedging in it, which reads as evasive, and learners who are honest about the reason produce one that is often too informative. Setting the two stages forces the check: after writing, what is the last thing the reader remembers, and is it the yes or the no. That check is the transferable part, and it catches both failure modes, because a message that is all hedge and a message that explains too much fail it in opposite directions.
questions.hint: Ask which half of your own message the reader would repeat afterwards.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Describing a colleague for a reference
questions.learningObjective: write a description whose adjectives can each be illustrated
questions.stem: Stage one: describe a colleague in three Spanish sentences for a job reference. Stage two: say what each of your adjectives commits you to proving.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: She has worked with me for three years and took over the accounts when I was away. She is responsable: she was the only one who could find the missing invoices that year. She is tranquila under pressure, because in the week the system failed she kept telling the rest of the team what to do. Stage two: the first adjective commits the writer to a story about reliability, and the second to a story about conduct under difficulty, and those are different claims with different evidence. An adjective such as buena or eficiente commits the writer to nothing, because no story illustrates either and the reader is left with a word that could describe anybody. That is the practical test to apply to a description: for each adjective, ask what happened, and if nothing happened then the adjective is a filler. A third stage, which is not asked for here, would be to cut any adjective with no story, since a shorter description with three illustrations beats a long one with six empty words.

questions.explanation: The two stages test different things and the second one is where the learning is. A learner asked to describe somebody produces adjectives because adjectives are what descriptions are made of, and the words are usually chosen for how positive they sound rather than for what they claim. Asking what each adjective commits the writer to proving converts a list of praise into a set of obligations, and the most common result is that two words survive and the rest are cut. That is the point of the item, since the instinct to add more praise is what makes a reference unusable, and shortening a description is a harder skill than lengthening one.
questions.hint: For each adjective, ask what happened, and cut the ones with no story behind them.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Planning a trip and choosing the constructions
questions.learningObjective: plan a future arrangement and justify the tenses chosen
questions.stem: Stage one: describe a plan for a trip in three Spanish sentences, using a different future construction in each. Stage two: say which of the three claims the strongest commitment and why.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: Voy a pedir las entradas esta semana, porque ya sé las fechas. Iré en autobús, aunque quizá vaya en tren si el billete sale más barato. Si hace buen tiempo, me quedaré unos días más. Stage two: the strongest commitment is the first, because the construction reports an intention that is already under way and the sentence gives evidence for it, the dates being known. The second is weaker because it is set against a condition and a doubt in the same breath, and a speaker who says quizá is not promising. The third looks decisive and is not, because a whole clause is put behind a condition that nobody has checked, and in Spanish a condition governs the whole statement that follows it. The general point for a learner is that the future has a scale, and the scale is chosen by how settled the plan is, not by style: a settled intention takes the first construction, a prediction about a fact takes the second, and anything behind an if should not be dressed up as a promise.

questions.explanation: The second stage is the one that teaches, because a learner can produce three future sentences without having any idea what any of them commits them to. Asking which is strongest forces the comparison the learner would otherwise make by feel, and it exposes the commonest error, which is to reach for the most decisive looking construction in order to sound confident. A conditional in Spanish is not a decoration around a promise; it is a statement about what has not been established. Setting the two stages also gives a natural place to mention the past, since a plan that was made and has not happened yet is the third category and the one learners reach for first.
questions.hint: Rank your own three sentences, and ask which one another person could rely on.
